Complete: “We ___ dinner when the lights ___ out.” Use have and go. Then combine these events so their order is clear: I left my ticket at home; later, I realised this at the station.

body.note: Suggested answer: “We were having dinner when the lights went out.” For the second task: “At the station, I realised I had left my ticket at home.” Having dinner is the background; went out is the event. Leaving the ticket happened before realising it.

body.key: Use tense and time markers together to distinguish background, main events and earlier events.

chapters.title: Travel arrangements: booking, checking in and handling changes
chapters.subtitle: Understand reservations and ask for practical help when plans change.

body.p: A reservation is an arrangement to keep a room, seat or service for you. When you arrive, staff may ask for the name on the booking or a booking reference. Keep your questions specific: ask whether breakfast is included, what time check-out is, or where a replacement service leaves from. These details help you act on the answer.

Some travel verbs have related nouns with different forms: you check in, but the process is check-in; a flight takes off, and its departure from the ground is take-off. Learn the phrase as well as the word. A delayed service is later than planned; a cancelled service will not run as scheduled. Luggage is normally uncountable: say two bags or two pieces of luggage.

list: “I have a reservation under the name Morgan” identifies your booking.
“Is breakfast included?” asks whether it is part of the room price.
“Has the departure time changed?” asks for an updated time.
“Where does the replacement bus leave from?” asks for its departure point.

body.p: Receptionist: “Good evening. Do you have a reservation?” Guest: “Yes, under the name Morgan.” Receptionist: “Two nights, is that right?” Guest: “That’s right. Is breakfast included?” Receptionist: “Yes. It starts at seven.” Guest: “And what time is check-out?” Receptionist: “Eleven.” Later, the guest learns that the return train is cancelled and asks where the replacement bus leaves from.
Your train is delayed, but no new departure time is shown. Write a question asking for an update. Then ask a hotel to confirm that your reservation is for two nights.

body.note: Suggested answer: “Do you know the new departure time?” and “Could you confirm that my reservation is for two nights?” Ask about the information that is missing instead of assuming delayed means cancelled.

body.key: Separate booking details from changes to the service, and ask for the specific information you need.

chapters.title: Resolving a complaint: facts, impact and a clear request
chapters.subtitle: Describe a service problem firmly and ask for a specific remedy.

body.p: An effective complaint helps the reader understand what happened and what would resolve it. Anger may explain why you are writing, but a sequence of facts makes the issue easier to investigate. Include the relevant reference, the expected service, the actual outcome and the practical impact. Then state a realistic request without hiding it in a long paragraph.

Distinguish describing a problem from accusing someone of causing it deliberately. “The package arrived with two items missing” reports an outcome; “You deliberately removed two items” adds a claim about intention. For requests, “I would appreciate it if you could…” is polite and clear when followed by a specific action. “Despite” takes a noun or -ing form; “although” introduces a clause.

list: “I am writing regarding order 482” identifies the subject.
“The confirmation stated three items, but only one arrived” contrasts expectation and outcome.
“As a result, we could not complete the planned work” explains the impact.
“Please confirm when the missing items can be sent” requests a concrete next step.

body.p: “I am writing regarding order 482, delivered on Monday. The confirmation listed three notebooks, but the package contained only one. As a result, two participants did not receive their materials. I would appreciate it if you could send the missing notebooks or explain the available alternatives. Please confirm the next step by Thursday.” The message is firm without asserting an unproven intention.

Rewrite “Your service is terrible. Fix it!” as a short complaint about a parcel that arrived three days late. Include one consequence and one request. Then correct “Despite the parcel was late, we used it.”

body.note: Suggested answer: Example: “The parcel arrived three days after the confirmed date, so we could not use it at the event. Please explain what options are available to resolve this.” For the second task: “Although the parcel was late, we used it” or “Despite the delay, we used it.”

body.key: Make the facts, impact and requested next step explicit; do not present assumptions about intention as facts.

chapters.title: Comparing options: criteria, degree and justified choices
chapters.subtitle: Explain why an option suits a purpose instead of calling it simply better.

body.p: A useful comparison begins with a purpose. A lighter bag may suit a walking trip, while a larger bag may suit moving equipment. Without a criterion, “better” tells your listener very little. Name the qualities that matter, compare the options on those qualities, and explain which trade-off you are willing to accept.

Modify comparatives with words such as slightly, considerably or much: “slightly lighter”, “considerably cheaper”. Do not normally use very directly before a comparative; say “much better”, not “very better”. “Not as… as” compares a lower degree of a quality: “A is not as spacious as B.” “Whereas” introduces a contrasting clause, while “unlike” is commonly followed by a noun phrase.

list: “A is slightly lighter than B” describes a small difference.
“B is twice as expensive as A” means B costs two times as much.
“Whereas A is portable, B offers more storage” contrasts two features.
“On balance, A suits our needs better” introduces a considered overall choice.

body.p: “Bag A costs 40 units and weighs 600 grams. Bag B costs 80 units and weighs 900 grams, but holds more equipment. B is twice as expensive as A, whereas A is 300 grams lighter. For a short walking trip, I would choose A because low weight matters more than extra space. For moving bulky equipment, I would reconsider.” The recommendation follows the stated purpose.

A room costs 60 units per night and another costs 90. The cheaper room is smaller but closer to your workplace. Write two comparative sentences and a recommendation for someone who values a short journey to work. Avoid claiming that either room is best for everyone.

body.note: Suggested answer: “The second room is 50 % more expensive than the first. The first is not as spacious, but it is closer to work. I would choose it if a short journey is the priority.” Note that 90 is 1.5 times 60, not twice 60.

body.key: A justified choice connects comparative language to criteria and the user’s purpose.

chapters.title: Building an argument: concessions, counterarguments and scope
chapters.subtitle: Acknowledge a strong objection and show how it changes your conclusion.

body.p: A persuasive argument does more than collect reasons for a preferred conclusion. It recognises the strongest relevant objection and explains how that objection affects the recommendation. A concession acknowledges a valid point without necessarily accepting the opposing conclusion. It becomes useful when the next sentence shows what follows from it.

“Admittedly” introduces a point you accept; “nevertheless” signals that another consideration still supports your position. “Even if” grants a hypothetical condition without asserting that it is true, whereas “even though” presents the concession as a fact. Keep the scope of your claim proportionate: recommending a limited trial does not require proving that permanent adoption will succeed everywhere.

list: “Admittedly, the initial cost is substantial” recognises a genuine drawback.
“That objection is valid insofar as it concerns the first month” limits the area of agreement.
“Even if demand remains unchanged, the trial could answer the access question” considers a hypothetical case.
“This supports a pilot, rather than immediate full adoption” states the scope of the conclusion.

body.p: “Extending library hours could improve access for evening students. Admittedly, additional staffing would have a cost, and the number of likely users is uncertain. Nevertheless, a four-week trial on one evening per week would allow the library to measure demand before making a permanent commitment. This supports a limited experiment, not a claim that longer hours will necessarily pay for themselves.” The objection helps shape the proposal.

A proposal to open a study room earlier faces an objection about staffing. Write a concession and a narrowed recommendation. Then explain the difference between “Even if attendance is low…” and “Even though attendance is low…”.

body.note: Suggested answer: “Admittedly, earlier opening would require staff time. A short trial on two mornings would allow us to assess use before expanding the schedule.” Even if considers low attendance hypothetically; even though presents low attendance as a fact in the argument.

body.key: A strong counterargument should influence the reasoning or scope of your conclusion, not merely appear in a token sentence.

chapters.title: Editing for precision: ambiguity, reference and parallel structure
chapters.subtitle: Make relationships between ideas clear without changing the intended meaning.

body.p: A sentence can be grammatically acceptable and still leave a reader unsure who acted, what a pronoun refers to or which condition applies. Editing for precision means locating these competing interpretations and choosing wording that makes the intended relationship explicit. You are not simply making sentences longer or more formal.

Pronouns need clear reference. “When Lina spoke to Sara, she was concerned” leaves the identity of she uncertain without context. Modifiers also need a clear target: “Only Lina reviewed the report” differs from “Lina reviewed only the report”. Parallel structure helps a list reveal comparable actions. After “The role involves”, use matching forms such as planning, reviewing and reporting.

list: Replace a pronoun with a name or noun when two plausible referents compete.
Place only close to the element it restricts, checking the intended contrast.
Keep coordinated actions in parallel grammatical forms.
After editing, verify that you preserved the intended meaning rather than choosing one silently.

body.p: Draft: “When Lina spoke to Sara, she said only the report needed updating and asked her to check the figures and reviewing the appendix.” Before revising, establish who spoke and who should check. If Lina made both requests to Sara, write: “Lina told Sara that only the report needed updating. Lina asked Sara to check the figures and review the appendix.” The second sentence also makes the coordinated verbs parallel.

Revise “When Omar emailed Ben, he was worried” to make Ben the worried person. Then correct “The role involves planning lessons, to review exercises and giving feedback.” Finally, explain the restriction in “Only Omar edited the summary”.

body.note: Suggested answer: “Ben was worried when Omar emailed him.” The list becomes “planning lessons, reviewing exercises and giving feedback”. Only Omar restricts the person: no one else edited the summary in the relevant context. It does not mean the summary was the only thing Omar edited.

body.key: Precision comes from clear reference, modifier placement and parallel structure, checked against the intended meaning.
